\begin{figure}[tb]

    \caption{The Bellman dynamic-programming table $g_i(s)$ for the didactic instance $a = (1, \ldots, 6)$: each cell counts the subsets of the first $i$ weights that sum to $s$, computed exactly by the counting recursion, and the highlighted final row is the degeneracy profile $g(T)$. The table is computed inline and is deterministic. It supports the benchmark's validation logic: at the production weight scale $a_i = O(n^{2})$ the lattice of reachable sums is polynomially wide, so dynamic programming produces the exact degeneracy profile in polynomial time and serves as the validation reference for every reconstructed read. It equally fixes what the benchmark is not - a pseudo-polynomially tractable control, so no worst-case hardness is inherited from subset-sum, and nothing in the table establishes a separation between SSG and classical methods.}
